blocks.text: גוזל (see §. 1, note ***) denotes both the young and the year-old dove (cf. גוזל בן שנה, Gittin 56b), and with this name Rashi explains the פרידה occurring in B. mez. 84b, cf. §. 239.
The young that is not yet fledged is called: ניפול (Pullus, B. batra 23a).

Of this species of dove there are three varieties: a) יונה עליה, i.e., the dove that lives in the upper rooms of the house; b) יונה שובך, doves that are kept in dovecotes, and c) יונה הרדיסאות, doves which, like the first two kinds, live either in the house or in the dovecote, but differ from them in that they remain constantly in their dwelling and do not seek their food outside.

This distinction is drawn still more precisely as follows: the יונה עליה stays throughout the day in the field or elsewhere outside, and returns in the evening to the house, where a nest has been prepared for it in the upper rooms.

The יונה שובך likewise stays outside during the day, but returns at evening to the dovecote; both kinds were also accustomed to nest in holes in the rocks, or in jars that had been set into the city walls expressly for this purpose.

From both kinds the יונה הרדיסאות differs, which does not go away from the dovecote or from the house (Beza 24a). The latter name is explained either as a proper place name and accordingly also [p. 200] read הדרסיאות (in which case one should perhaps think of the southern part of the Lebanon range, inhabited by Druze, cf. Schwarz: חוצאות הארץ pag. 6), or as a personal name after King Herod (Chulin 139b). He is said, as Maimuni (Chulin 12, 1) says, to have been the first to attempt to domesticate doves*).

This last dove is thus the house dove (Columba domestica) in the most proper sense, and further differs from the first two kinds in that, owing to its training, it is more easily caught, whereas those flutter about in the dovecote or in the nest and are less easily seized (Beza 24a).

(Continuation). In some passages doves and ravens are set up as opposites. In Meharaba there were two families, one was called: בי יונה (House of the Dove), the other: בי עורבתי (House of the Raven); the former enjoyed respect, the other fell into contempt (Kiduschin 70b). Further it is related: There was a man who was versed in the language of birds; he fell into captivity and one day heard the call of a raven: “Ilisch, Ilisch, flee, flee!” But Ilisch, for so that man was named, said: “I do not believe the lying bird.”

Then a dove came and likewise called those words to him, whereupon Ilisch said: “This bird I believe, for Israel is compared to the dove” (Gittin 45a). The faculty of speech of animals is treated in §. 39; here we take from the two Talmud passages only the point that the raven is cunning and thievish, whereas the dove is gentle and mild, and it is the Midrash especially that richly exploits the comparison of Israel with the dove; of the many passages we refer only to Midr. Rabba Schir ha-Schirim fol. 12, col. 4.

The dove is persecuted more than any other by other birds, while it itself does harm to none; but precisely for this reason it, an image of quiet gentleness, is deemed worthy among all birds to be chosen for sacrifice (B. Kama 93a), and, [p. 201] since it lives in the strictest monogamy, it serves as a symbol of chastity (Erubin 100b). That comparison of Israel with the dove is frequently expressed in the Talmud and is variously presented by the commentaries. Rashi (on Sabbat 130a) says: The dove does not defend itself with its beak like other birds, but with its wings, and further (on Berachoth 53b): The dove either flies away or defends itself with its wings, and what the wings are to the dove, the Law is to Israel, by which it preserves and maintains itself in all persecutions.

The Tosephot (Sabbat 49a, s.v. כנפיה), on the other hand, explain that every other bird, when it is tired, settles down to rest, whereas the dove lets one wing rest while it flies on with the other; thus Israel seeks strength in its persecution. As regards this latter point of natural history, it is well known that doves sometimes fly up and down for several hours, and the bird of prey in their vicinity flies off without booty after vain exertion; the muscular strength of the dove must therefore indeed be great.

From the Midrash passage mentioned above we take only the point that the dove does not leave the dovecote even when its young are taken from it. This assertion is not shared by Buffon. He regards the doves of our dovecotes as always only half-domesticated animals, for they like to live in larger company, and thus sometimes leave their abode.
We note only further that that Midrash passage also mentions the decoy dove; it says there: In the dovecote a dove was fed which by its scent*) lured other doves to it.
